name: Zoe Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Zoe, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to Brookside around seven, after Daniel's gone off on the early bus route. First job is the hens, letting them out and collecting eggs, then the pigs, which I'm still a bit nervous with, if I'm honest. Thursdays and Fridays are box days, so we're in the packing barn weighing out carrots and kale for about two hundred households.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a care worker for twenty-two years, mostly nights, and my back and my sleep gave out. A friend from the choir volunteered at Brookside, I went along, and when they got funding for a paid farm assistant, I applied. I was fifty-six when I started, the oldest trainee they'd ever had.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and the worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is being outside and seeing the families come for their boxes, the kids running to see the piglets. Worst is how much I still don't know. Our grower, Mateo, can look at a leaf and tell you what's wrong, and I'm still checking the book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, that's a relief, now can we talk about something that matters, like the price of feed. At the trust meetings I'd say it out loud. I might put a little post on the farm's page, something like, still no robot can pick a good leek.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would mean my life carries on as planned. I'd work here till sixty-five or so, Daniel would keep driving, and we'd get by. I use the AI thing now and then to tidy up the newsletter, and if that's all it ever is, that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and finally get properly good at the pigs. I'd ask the trust if I could do the livestock course at the agricultural college, one day a week over winter. And we'd keep putting a bit by, the hundred and fifty a month we manage now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, like when everyone tells you a storm's coming and you get drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to talk about feed prices. Why that, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what actually keeps us up at night at Brookside. Feed went up nearly a third in two years, and the trust nearly had to sell the pigs. A plateau doesn't fix that, it just means nothing new to fix it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that would be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small part. I'd hoped these tools might do the boring bits, the box spreadsheets and the funding forms, so Mateo and I could spend more time on the land. If it's all hype, we're still doing forms on a Sunday night.

S0.say: I'd say it's a relief and that we should get back to what matters, like the price of feed. I might post on the farm's page that no robot can pick a good leek.
S0.think: Her life carries on as planned: work at Brookside until about 65 while Daniel keeps driving. She'd be slightly disappointed that the tools won't take over the funding forms.
S0.do: Keeps working at Brookside and asks the trust to fund a one-day-a-week livestock course at the agricultural college over winter. Keeps saving about 150 a month.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a forecast storm that turns into drizzle.
S0.quote: If it's all hype, we're still doing forms on a Sunday night.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe frames even the calm picture through the farm's real money troubles, especially feed prices. She is neither a fan nor a critic of AI; she hoped it would take the paperwork. Getting good at the pigs is her own measure of success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should make sure the changes help small farms and the workers, not just the big operations. At the trust I'd argue for any new kit to be shared between farms in the area, like a co-op. I'd say that at the farmers' market too, to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Brookside is one of the safer places to be. We're not there to make the most money, we're there to grow food and bring people in. They'd buy a weeding robot before they'd let me go, I think, and that might even help my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which tools the other farms round here actually get on with. Once the Carvers' farm or someone has used a weeding robot for a season, I'd ask to go and watch it. And I'd start using the AI more for the pig records, because Mateo already does and it's saved him hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not for me so much as for Daniel, because bus driving is one of those jobs everyone says will change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've got a few years, love, and you're sixty-one, you might just make it. He'd joke that he'll teach the bus to sing to the old ladies the way he does. He knows every passenger on the 14 by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join anything, a group or a campaign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for the trust's members' board, I think. It's been on my mind anyway, and if decisions about machines are coming, I want a farm worker in the room. Not a big march, just a vote at the table.

S1.say: I'd say the changes should help small farms and their workers, and that new kit should be shared between farms like a co-op. I'd say it at the trust and the farmers' market.
S1.think: She thinks Brookside is a fairly safe place because it's there to grow food and bring people in. A weeding robot might even help her back; she worries more about Daniel's bus job.
S1.do: Waits a season to see which machines neighbouring farms get on with, then asks to watch them work. Starts using AI for the pig records and stands for the trust's members' board.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on Daniel's behalf rather than her own.
S1.quote: They'd buy a weeding robot before they'd let me go, I think, and that might even help my back.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe's steadiness shows in the order of her plans: watch the neighbours for a season, then adopt. She trusts her employer's values more than market logic. Her progressive leanings come out as co-ops and a seat on the board rather than protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in now, not later, with a proper income for people whose work disappears. I'd sign every petition going. And I'd say, quite loudly at the trust meeting, that we can't let the land just go to whoever owns the most robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it frightens me. Two years means I'm sixty when it lands, and Daniel's sixty-three. If my job and his job both go at once, we have about four months of money, and then what? The trust runs on grants, and grants vanish first in a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, no more takeaways on a Friday, cancel the streaming, put every spare penny aside. I'd talk to our son Idris about whether he could help with the mortgage if it came to it. When it arrived, I'd apply for whatever support was set up, and I'd go to the meetings to push for it to be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the same feeling as the night a resident fell on my shift. Your heart's going and you're doing things, but you know it's bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you do in the very first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Daniel at the kitchen table with the bank statements and actually look, which we never do. Then I'd ring my sister in Leeds, because she went through redundancy and knows the forms. Boring things, but that's where you start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said Brookside felt safe. Does it still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this one. In the slow picture the trust has time to adapt. In two years, the funders would be panicking about their own jobs, and nobody's paying for a fifty-eight-year-old trainee to learn pigs. I didn't leave twenty-two years of night shifts to end up as the human backup for a weeding machine.

S2.say: I'd say the government must step in now with a proper income for people whose work disappears, and that the land can't go to whoever owns the most robots.
S2.think: It frightens her: she'd be 60 and Daniel 63, both jobs could go at once, and they have about four months of savings. The trust runs on grants, which vanish first in a crisis.
S2.do: Cuts takeaways and streaming in the first week and goes through the bank statements with Daniel. Asks her son Idris about help with the mortgage and applies for support when it arrives, while pushing at meetings for it to be enough.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the night a resident fell on her shift: busy, heart racing, knowing it's bad.
S2.quote: Nobody's paying for a fifty-eight-year-old trainee to learn pigs.
S2.fieldNote: The speed collapses Zoe's sense that Brookside is a shelter, because grants dry up first. The double hit to her and Daniel is what moves her from uneasy to alarmed. Her first steps are practical and small, the habits of a care worker in a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them, and I'd mean the trust, the council and the government. I'd say it in the members' meetings: let's plan now how Brookside keeps people working alongside whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three. That's close enough to retirement that I could see a way through, maybe go part time at the end. Daniel would be sixty-six, and he could take his pension. So it's tight, but not the cliff edge of the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder from the start, two hundred and fifty a month instead of a hundred and fifty, and pay off the last bit of the car. Once a couple of the bigger farms had robots working, I'd learn to run ours, because someone at Brookside would have to. I'd also ask Mateo to teach me the planning side, the crop rotations, because that's the head work they'd still need a person for, at least for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can handle. It's a worry with a to-do list attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns panic into a plan. With two years I'm reacting. With five, Daniel retires before it hits, our mortgage has two years left instead of five, and I've got maybe a year's savings. Those three years are the difference between the bank and us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still campaign, like in the fast picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but differently. I'd write to the council about a scheme to keep small farms going as places for people, not just food factories. I'm not one for marches, but I can write a letter that gets read.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so the trust, the council and the government should use them to plan how farms keep people working alongside the machines.
S3.think: Five years takes her to 63, close enough to retirement to see a way through, maybe part time at the end. Daniel could take his pension at 66, so it's tight but not a cliff.
S3.do: Raises savings to about 250 a month from the start and pays off the car. Learns to run the farm's robots once bigger farms have them working, asks Mateo to teach her crop planning, and writes to the council about a small-farm scheme.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, a worry with a to-do list attached.
S3.quote: Those three years are the difference between the bank and us.
S3.fieldNote: The warning time maps neatly onto Zoe's household dates: Daniel's pension, the last years of the mortgage. She still waits for others to go first with the machines but commits to learning them. Her politics stay in letters and committees rather than the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a generation's worth of warning, so nobody has an excuse. At the farm I'd say let's make Brookside a place where people come to learn how to work with these machines. That's the sort of thing I'd put on the farm's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it would probably be fine. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, with Daniel, maybe still coming in to help with the hens on a Tuesday. It's my kids I'd think about. Idris is an electrician and Amina's a nursing assistant, and they'd be in their forties when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Brookside and learn the new tools as they come in, a season behind everyone else, like I always do. We'd keep saving steadily. And I'd have a proper talk with Amina about whether she wants to go on to train as a nurse, because I think the jobs with people's hands and hearts in them will last longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for the children than for me. Mostly I'd feel lucky with my timing, for once in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: For once? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've always been late for things. Late to get married, late to buy a house, late to farming at fifty-six. With this, being old is finally an advantage. It's a strange thing to be grateful for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Amina's studies. What would you actually say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, I'm not telling you what to do, but in ten years someone will still need to hold an old woman's hand at three in the morning. I know because I was that someone for twenty-two years. A robot can lift her, but it can't sit with her.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a generation's warning, so there's no excuse, and Brookside could become a place where people learn to work with the machines.
S4.think: For her it would probably be fine, since she'd be retired at 68. She thinks more about her children, an electrician and a nursing assistant, who'd be in their forties.
S4.do: Carries on at Brookside, learning new tools a season behind others, and keeps saving steadily. Talks to her daughter Amina about training as a full nurse.
S4.feel: Uneasy for her children but lucky with her own timing for once.
S4.quote: Being old is finally an advantage. It's a strange thing to be grateful for.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Zoe's worry moves entirely to her children, and her care-work past shapes the advice she'd give. Her line about always being late, and finally benefiting from it, was striking. Her steadiness is consistent: learn the tools, but a season behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both of us losing work at once, with four months in the bank. What would help is a public scheme that pays older people a fair wage to keep land like Brookside going, and honest warning early so families can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who looks after the animals when nobody's watching. On Christmas morning it's me and the pigs. Whatever comes, I hope someone still wants to be there on Christmas morning.

headlineQuote: I didn't leave twenty-two years of night shifts to end up as the human backup for a weeding machine.
portrait: Zoe Usman is 58 and has worked for two years at Brookside, a community land trust farm with vegetable boxes, pigs, hens and a few sheep, after 22 years of night shifts as a care worker. She is still learning, especially with the pigs, and uses AI now and then for the veg-box newsletter or a quick question about a sick animal. She believes in public support and shared ownership, and she wants proof before she changes anything. A plateau or steady change barely shakes her because the trust values people, but AGI in two years alarms her because both her job and her partner Daniel's bus driving would go at once. With five or ten years she settles into careful saving, learning the new tools once others have tested them, and planning a gentle exit around 65.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Daniel could both lose their work within two years, with only a few months of savings and their pensions still years away.
whatWouldHelp: A public scheme that pays older rural workers a fair wage to keep land like Brookside going, and honest, early notice so households can plan.
